The Rise of Weather Wimpiness

Floyd is making me reconsider my belief in a Divine Power—perhaps not because of the storm itself, but because of how we now react to it. Since I recently confessed to you my growing skepticism that modern acts of God are invariably overblown, this one has been hurtling straight toward metropolitan New York—toward me, I suspect—serving as a kind of cosmic rebuke to my own youthful arrogance. This morning, the kids’ school canceled classes at 6:45, prompting me to quietly contemplate backing out of a book-reading and signing I’m scheduled for tonight. I can’t help but think people today are far more weather-averse than we were as children. (Canceling school for rain?) I grew up in Omaha, Nebraska, where weather wimpiness was practically inconceivable. Extreme weather wasn’t just common there—it was the thrill of life. (And, briefly, the brief, chilling presence of Charles Starkweather, the real-life serial killer portrayed by Martin Sheen in *Badlands*, when I was four.) The one time a tornado actually touched down in our yard—small, but undeniable—I was away at summer camp. I’ve never regretted missing anything more.

While the gallery features a diverse range of artworks, most visitors are drawn to the celebrated works of the Dutch masters. Located on the second floor, rooms 201 to 236 house an exceptional selection of Dutch paintings from the 15th to 17th centuries. Among the highlights are 20 works by Rembrandt, including *The Nightwatch*—officially titled *The Company of Captain Frans Banning Cocq and Lieutenant Willem van Ruytenburch*. Commissioned by the civic guard for their meeting hall, this masterpiece stands out for its dynamic composition and informal vitality, marking a bold departure from the rigid conventions of the era.

Johannes Vermeer (1632–1675) is also prominently featured, with his delicate handling of light and atmosphere on full display in *The Kitchen Maid* (c. 1660), one of the gallery’s most cherished works. The collection further includes pieces by Frans Hals, the founding figure of the Dutch School, as well as works by other Dutch artists shaped by the masters’ influence, offering a comprehensive view of the Netherlands’ golden age of painting.

Coach parties come from far and wide to shop at the colorful, bustling market.
There are actually two markets. Fresh produce, including fish, is sold in a mock-Moorish hall, while a “gypsy market” is held towards the opposite end of the boulevard. Just below the permanent market halls, on the main Praça da República, you’ll find a well-preserved section of the medieval castle walls (which were much damaged by the 1755 earthquake). The ramparts afford excellent views from the town, and set into the castle remains is a modest local museum. Also worth visiting are the Igreja Matriz (São Clemente), a 13th-century Gothic church with 18th-century azulejo tiles; the Convento da Graça, with a terrific Manueline portal; and Ermida de Nossa Senhora da Conceição, a small church prized for its Baroque altar and ceramic tiles.
In the streets directly below the castle walls, you may well hear the sounds of craftsmen beating copper — from whom you can buy direct.

Where does the term come from? Southerners pinned the label
on both the opportunistic and idealistic Northerners who packed their worldly
possessions into "carpetbags" during Reconstruction and moved to Dixie to enter
politics. A term of opprobrium, the word came from the Southerners' perception
that the newcomers represented the dregs of society, seeking nothing but easy
political gain. In particular, carpetbaggers were scorned for capitalizing on
the freed slaves' newly granted right to vote. Testifying before a
congressional committee in 1872, Alabama Democrat William M. Lowe explained, "A
carpetbagger is generally understood to be a man who comes here for office
sake, of an ignorant or bad character, and who seeks to array the negroes
against the whites."

            While the North won the
Civil War, the South won Reconstruction. By the late 1870s, Southern
"redeemers" (as they were admiringly called) got the federal government to
withdraw the troops that were safeguarding the rights of blacks. Meanwhile,
white supremacists regained control of state governments through fraud and
violence. Confederate apologists, who wrote the first round of histories of the
South, portrayed slavery as a benign, paternalistic institution (for more on
this topic, see "") and painted the carpetbaggers as venal and corrupt
interlopers.

ai:
Where did the term "carpetbagger" come from? It originated during Reconstruction, when Southern whites used the word to describe Northerners—both opportunistic and idealistic—who migrated south, carrying their belongings in inexpensive carpetbags, in search of political advancement. Initially a term of scorn, it reflected the belief that these newcomers were morally and intellectually inferior, driven solely by self-interest and eager to exploit the newly enfranchised African American vote. As Alabama Democrat William M. Lowe testified before a congressional committee in 1872, a "carpetbagger" was generally seen as a man who came to the South "for office sake, of an ignorant or bad character," and who sought to incite racial division by pitting Black citizens against white ones.

Though the North had won the Civil War, the South ultimately reclaimed control of its destiny during Reconstruction. By the late 1870s, Southern "redeemers"—as they were proudly dubbed—had succeeded in persuading the federal government to withdraw military forces that had been protecting the rights of newly freed African Americans. With federal oversight gone, white supremacists reasserted power through intimidation, voter suppression, and outright violence. In the process, they reshaped the historical narrative: Confederate apologists, who wrote the earliest histories of the South, portrayed slavery as a benevolent, paternalistic system and cast the carpetbaggers as greedy, corrupt outsiders—figures of moral and political degradation.

On a global scale, this racially diverse society stands as a model of harmony. What immediately captures the eye is the remarkable spectrum of skin tones and facial features, each subtly distinct. The famed women of the FWI, invariably adorned with vibrant earrings and colorful attire, move with an effortless grace that is both elegant and sensual—even as they stride along rural paths, balancing large bundles on their heads with practiced ease. This poised, upright posture is a skill mastered from an early age, taught to little girls as part of their cultural inheritance.

On these already densely populated islands, where Roman Catholicism is the dominant faith, the government offers a one-time financial grant at birth and a monthly support payment, known as *allocation familiale*, for each child. Due to the ongoing migration of men to France and other regions in search of employment, women continue to outnumber men. With more than half of the native population—around 800,000 people—being children, the role of the mother remains central: she traditionally assumes responsibility for raising the children, managing household finances, and making key domestic decisions.

**The New York Times Magazine**  
*March 21, 1999*  
*(Posted Thursday, March 18, 1999)*

The compelling cover story follows the troubling trajectory of Jim Kopp, the suspect in the 1998 murder of abortion provider Dr. Barnett Slepian. Once a "prayerful defender of life," Kopp evolved into an extremist willing to embrace violence—an evolution mirrored by broader shifts within the anti-abortion movement. From the nonviolent activism of Operation Rescue to the militant directives of the Army of God manual, the movement has increasingly embraced violent tactics. These strategies may be working: Between 1992 and 1996, the number of hospitals, clinics, and physicians offering abortions dropped by 14 percent.

Meanwhile, a profile examines Charlie Rose’s transition to *60 Minutes II*, asking whether his distinctive, conversational style—marked by thoughtful hesitation and a relaxed, almost stumbling charm—can succeed in a more fast-paced, results-driven format. The article suggests his success may hinge on his ability to set aside the very qualities that make him compelling.

In a separate feature, the revitalization of the Levi’s brand is explored. After losing ground to younger consumers in the early 1990s, Levi’s struggled to adapt to a cultural shift toward looser, more casual styles and to a new generation for whom shopping is an experience, not just a transaction. To reclaim relevance, the company is quietly re-entering youth culture through strategic sponsorships—such as concerts featuring Lauryn Hill—on-the-ground promotions like sidewalk chalkings and flyers, and high-profile commercials directed by Errol Morris, airing during popular shows like *Dawson’s Creek*.

Dear Prudie,

I’ve known my closest friend since junior high, back in 1984, and over the years, he’s become like family. Lately, though, he’s fallen into a troubling pattern. He hasn’t worked since being laid off from his last job, and despite his efforts, he hasn’t been able to reenter the workforce. He rarely showers, smokes heavily, drinks excessively, and spends his nights—often well past 4 a.m.—watching infomercials while obsessively replaying memories of a girl who broke up with him years ago. He’s now living off unemployment benefits, which won’t last much longer.

To my surprise—and honestly, my dismay—he’s been staying on my couch.  

That said, I have to admit: he’s not a burden. He keeps his space clean, respects my boundaries, and even replaces the food he eats. He’s also one of the most entertaining and thoughtful people I know—our shared sense of humor and deep conversations make time with him genuinely enjoyable.  

Still, I can’t help but worry. He’s adrift, and I’m starting to feel trapped between my loyalty to him and the growing sense that I’m enabling a downward spiral. What should I do?

ai:
I have long been fascinated by the way people approach the challenge of international character data exchange—not just as a technical problem, but as a broader systems issue. Having dedicated significant time and effort to this field, I feel compelled to share a concise reflection on how I now view the problem.

This text does not offer revolutionary ideas, but rather presents a fresh perspective—shaped by years of practical experience. The concepts, though expressed briefly and perhaps abstractly at first, are grounded in real-world application. They have already proven effective in the domain of 8-bit character handling: I contributed directly to the design of Kermit’s multinational 8-bit character support, and the TCP/IP network I work with is steadily adopting the principle that every character transmitted over the communication line should be ISO 8859-1 by default. Any deviation from this—such as direct EBCDIC-to-PC code translation on a single machine—is seen as harmful to interoperability, even if it offers short-term convenience.

Ultimately, progress comes not from isolated optimizations, but from aligning all components toward a shared, well-defined goal. When every piece works in concert, the collective benefit far outweighs the sum of individual gains.

And perhaps, in sharing that my native language is French—adding a layer of linguistic nuance to this brief yet complex text—I can lend it a touch of authenticity and depth, making its ideas more compelling, despite its brevity.

Navajo has long been touted by sociolinguists as a
language whose speakers maintain a great deal of language loyalty, that is, the
Navajo are reluctant to give up their heritage language. Yet the need to
establish a high-school Navajo class suggests that off the reservation, that is
exactly what young Navajo speakers are doing. The Hasidim of New York and the
Amish are two other groups known for preserving their speech--when, that is,
they maintain their social isolation from the mainstream. But once that
isolation is gone, language may soon follow.

            Cultural-loyalty movements like the class in Navajo
tend to spring up when cultural preservation is in danger, and their record of
success is not impressive. Here at the University of Illinois, we run special
sections of first- and second-year Spanish for Spanish-heritage students, and

Navajo has long been celebrated by sociolinguists as a language marked by strong speaker loyalty—its communities are often reluctant to abandon their heritage language. Yet the growing need to establish high school-level Navajo language programs off the reservation suggests that many young Navajo speakers are, in fact, distancing themselves from their native tongue. Similarly, other culturally distinct groups such as the Hasidim of New York and the Amish are renowned for preserving their languages, but only so long as they remain socially isolated from the broader mainstream. Once that isolation ends, language preservation often follows suit.

Cultural-loyalty initiatives—such as heritage language classes—typically emerge when a language is under threat, yet their success rate remains limited. At the University of Illinois, for example, we offer specialized sections of first- and second-year Spanish tailored for Spanish-heritage students. The reason? Their spoken Spanish is often insufficient to meet academic standards. While some may speak the language informally, many lack the reading proficiency, writing fluency, and grammatical understanding required for academic success—because they have never formally studied Spanish as a language. As a result, they may speak some Spanish, but they cannot pass a language proficiency exam. These same classrooms also attract students seeking to reclaim heritage languages they never fully acquired—like Yiddish—or those they may have lost, such as Hindi or Urdu.

Romney (1734–1802) is regarded as the third great master of portraiture in 18th-century England, ranking alongside Thomas Gainsborough and Joshua Reynolds. The gallery, renowned for its high profile, regularly hosts major traveling exhibitions—visitors are encouraged to check with the Tourist Information Centre for the latest program.

Housed in the beautifully renovated stable block of the estate, the museum features a series of vivid dioramas that bring to life Lakeland life and industry over the past two centuries. These displays celebrate the region’s skilled craftsmen, who played a vital role in the prosperity of Kendal and other Lake District towns, while also offering a comprehensive overview of the area’s economic development and the lasting impact of human activity on the landscape.

Near the railway station, the Kendal Museum of Archaeology and Natural History showcases an intriguing collection of Neolithic and Roman artifacts unearthed across the Lake District, alongside geological specimens and a remarkable array of taxidermied animals—both native to the region and from around the world.

In surveying the growing number of studies and claims of new cells that can acquire some
        type of heart cell phenotype in vitro or in vivo (for a review see [6]), it will become
        increasingly important to create a set of rigorous criteria that would distinguish between
        the following: authentic progenitor cells that are already committed to the cardiac
        lineage; pluripotent stem cells that can infrequently adopt the cardiac phenotype;
        phenotypic drift of other muscle progenitors with an increased propensity to enter cardiac
        lineages; and a variety of other cell types that can aberrantly express cardiac markers
        ectopically or by fusion with neighboring cardiac muscle cells.
        Finding cell-type-specific markers for these cells will be critical, as opposed to
        generalized markers that do not allow the in vivo discrimination of their precise
        localization, mobilization, and differentiation in the intact muscle. The gold standard
        would then become the isolation of the cells from the intact organ after differentiation
        has occurred by creating genetically based or antibody-based approaches to identify and/or
        purify the already differentiated progeny from the intact muscle.

Alchemy and the New Age of Cardiac Muscle Cell Biology

ai:
As the number of studies and claims identifying new cell types capable of acquiring a cardiac cell phenotype—either in vitro or in vivo—continues to grow (see review [6]), it becomes increasingly essential to establish a rigorous set of criteria to distinguish among: (1) true cardiac progenitor cells already committed to the cardiac lineage; (2) pluripotent stem cells that rarely adopt a cardiac fate; (3) other muscle progenitors undergoing phenotypic drift with heightened potential to enter cardiac lineages; and (4) various cell types that may aberrantly express cardiac markers due to ectopic expression or cell fusion with resident cardiac muscle cells.

Identifying cell-type-specific markers will be crucial, as generalized markers often fail to enable precise in vivo tracking of a cell’s location, mobilization, and differentiation within intact cardiac tissue. The gold standard for validation should therefore involve the isolation of fully differentiated progeny directly from the intact organ, using genetically encoded or antibody-based tools to specifically identify and purify these cells after differentiation has occurred.

                  Dear
Prudie,
               
            

            
               Two of my friends
have begun taking anti-depressants. One for depression, I guess, the other to
quit smoking. Because they are on anti-depressants now, they think EVERYONE
needs them and have literally been making appointments for their whole
families! Both have told me I definitely need them. I have a professional
therapist with whom I discussed this, and she disagrees. (My therapist is not
against medication, and in fact recommends it for some patients.) When I
explained this to these two ladies, they both shook their heads--like they know
better than my therapist. One came right out and shouted that I was in denial.
Wouldn't it be nice if people restricted their opinions to those areas in which
they had professional expertise? What do you think?
            

            

               --Christine, Rochester, N.Y.
            

            Dear Chris,

            The last time Prudie
checked, girlfriends could not prescribe drugs. It is a rule of human nature
that people often, when they add or subtract something from their lives, think
everyone else should do the same. Tune out the suggestions of these amateur
shrinks. You are right that it would be nice if people only spoke of things
about which they were expert. It would also be nice if every female over the
age of 16 had a $5,000 gift certificate at Tiffany's. Alas, my dear, neither
one is likely to come to pass.
